claim: Multilayer nonlinear ONN image encoder (Wang et al., Nat. Photon. 17, 408 (2023)): maximum image compression ratio at which tasks still worked
quote: demonstrate that the nonlinear ONN pre-processor can achieve compression ratios of up to 800:1 - corresponding to compressing the input to just a two-dimensional output vector
notes: Reduction in pixels read = the compression ratio: 1,600 input pixels -> 2 detector values. No energy per inference reported anywhere in the paper (negative finding); the optical-to-optical nonlinearity is a powered commercial image intensifier whose power is not given. Tier next (lab).

claim: Same ONN encoder, QuickDraw 10-class at 196:1 (4 detector values per 28x28 image): accuracy vs linear optical and best all-digital linear encoder with the same 4-value bottleneck
quote: multilayer nonlinear ONN encoder's performance (79% test accuracy) robustly surpasses that of linear encoders, beating both the optical (69.5%) and optimized digital (74%) single-layer
notes: The electronic baseline is a linear encoder with the same bottleneck, not a full-resolution digital CNN; paper says the ONN is 'slightly worse than digital neural networks with similar architectures'. Readouts: 4 instead of 784 (196:1).

claim: Same ONN encoder, flow-cytometry cell-organelle classification (5 classes) at an effective 400:1 compression
quote: compresses the input images by an effective ratio of 400:1, and results in a classification accuracy for the 5 considered classes that is better than the linear-ONN sensor (93% vs 88.5% test accuracy
notes: Images were binarized and displayed on a DMD (lab emulation of a scene), not captured from a live sample.

claim: Same ONN encoder operates directly on broadband, spatially incoherent visible light (intensity-domain, non-negative weights)
quote: Imaging applications typically involve broadband, incoherent ambient light, so our device was designed to operate directly on broadband, incoherent visible light images.
notes: Incoherence handling: non-negative intensity weights on an LCD after microlens fan-out ('the modulation of the intensity of a spatial mode by an LCD pixel corresponds to product between two non-negative numbers', Supp. Note 2). Etendue: free-space multimode path, no waveguide coupling.

claim: Same ONN encoder: measured optical transmission of one matrix-vector multiplier
locator: arXiv v1, Supplementary Note (optical transmission measurement)
quote: The overall transmission of one optical matrix-vector multiplier was measured to be 2.9% at best.
notes: ~35x photon loss per optical layer. Same note: 'the optical loss of the current proof-of-concept experimental setup still cannot support low-light operation'. This is the photon cost of the fan-out/intensity-mask approach.

claim: Scaling argument for optical pre-processing: C-fold fewer pixels gives ~C-fold better frame rate, photons per pixel, system power, size, weight and cost
quote: In a conventional image sensor, using a camera with C-fold fewer pixels typically leads to a C-fold improvement in achievable frame rate, number of photons per pixel, system power, size, weight, and cost
notes: An argument, not a measurement. It holds only if sensor/readout/transport energy dominates; R10-017 and R10-011 show cases where it does not.

claim: Angle-sensitive-pixel (ASP) CMOS sensor that optically computes Gabor edge filters (a first CNN layer): measured sensor power breakdown
value: 1.8 mW total (ADCs 100 uW) at 384x384 vs 428 mW for a 20 MP Sony smartphone sensor
quote: All numbers reported are from actual sensor measurements ... Total Power: 1.8 mW ... ADCs: 100
notes: Different resolutions and process nodes; authors warn the comparison is approximate. Frame rate not given in the table, so energy per pixel cannot be derived from it. Input: incoherent scene light through a lens; the grating response is an intensity (differential) filter. Tier next (fabricated prototype).

claim: ASP edge encoding cuts sensor output bandwidth 10:1 by storing non-zero edge coefficients
quote: For a traditional image sensor, 1.2 Mbits is needed to digitize 150Kpixels (384 x 384) at 8 bit resolution while ASPs only require 120Kbits.
notes: Prior-work measurement (ref. [54]); run-length encoding of sparse edges, i.e. the ADC is only turned on for edge pixels. Conversions removed ~90% of ADC events for natural scenes (scene-dependent).

claim: ASP Vision accuracy across MNIST, CIFAR-10/100, PF-83 relative to all-electronic baselines (simulated ASP responses)
quote: Across all datasets, ASP Vision was within 0.1-5.6% of the baseline accuracies.
notes: Accuracies are from simulation with the ASP filter model; the hardware prototype was used only for small real demos.

claim: ASP gratings lose light: relative quantum efficiency can drop to 10% (phase gratings reach ~50%)
quote: ASP pixels can suffer loss of light through the diffraction gratings as low as 10% relative quantum efficiency
notes: Photon cost of computing in the pixel optics; matters for dim or short-dwell scenes.

claim: Hybrid meta-optic + digital ANN at matched power and latency (Huang et al., Nanophotonics 13, 1191 (2024)): optics helps only at very small readout size
value: advantage only for N <= 8x8 readout values; identical accuracy above
quote: Keeping the latency and power constant between purely digital ANN and hybrid optical-digital ANN, we identified a low-power/ latency regime, where an optical encoder provides higher classification accuracy than a purely digital ANN.
notes: Results text: 'for N > 8 x 8, the digital and hybrid ANN demonstrate identical classification accuracies'. Negative for large-image EO: the photonic advantage appears only where overall accuracy is lower than achievable. Incoherent (OLED-projected green light).

claim: Same study: experimental accuracy gain of the optical encoder at small readout size N
quote: we found an increase in validation accuracy (~10%) with a hybrid optical-digital ANN
notes: At N = 3x3 the theory predicts up to ~20%; experiment ~10%. Lab scene = MNIST on an OLED monitor (~15 W, excluded from the budget by the authors).

claim: Energy analysis cited by Huang et al. (Colburn et al., Appl. Opt. 58, 3179 (2019)): a single optical conv layer gives no advantage unless the input is very large
value: no advantage (1 optical conv layer, small inputs)
quote: an analysis considering these energy costs shows that implementing only one convolutional layer in optics does not provide any advantage, unless the input has a very large dimension
notes: Secondary citation of an energy model (Colburn 2019, paywalled, not read). Supports: optics wins only when it removes readout of a very large input, i.e. EO-scale frames - but see R10-011 for the accuracy side.

claim: Compressed meta-optical encoder (Wirth-Singh et al., Adv. Photon. Nexus 2025): hybrid accuracy and electronic MACs vs all-electronic AlexNet-Mod
quote: experimentally achieves classification accuracy of 93.9% (± 0.25%) and 93.4% (± 0.22%) on the training and testing datasets, respectively, and requires only 85,824 MAC operations
notes: MAC reduction ~200x vs AlexNet-Mod, ~2.7x vs the compressed electronic net (228,672 MACs, >96%). Incoherent green light from a micro-LED display.

claim: Same meta-optical encoder: projected inference energy from MAC count at ~1 pJ/MAC
quote: the hybrid network is expected to reduce the required power to classify an input from 17uJ to 85nJ based on the reduction in MAC operations.
notes: Pure MAC-count x 1 pJ estimate; excludes sensor readout, which the authors say is unchanged (R10-016).

claim: Same meta-optical encoder removes MACs but no conversions: the full camera frame is still captured and digitised
quote: For input which is already in the optical domain, the power and latency required to capture an image and convert it to digital input is the same regardless of the network.
notes: Key distinction for H2: PSF-engineering encoders feeding a full image sensor save digital MACs, not ADC conversions or downlink bits. Only encoders that shrink the number of detector outputs (R10-001, R10-008, R10-051) remove conversions.

claim: Scene-agnostic compression with shift-invariant meta-optical encoders (simulation): lens imaging + pixel binning wins at low noise
value: lens-binning best at equal compression (low-noise regime)
quote: In the low-noise regime, lens-binning gives the highest reconstruction fidelity and strongest YOLOv8 detection metrics at the same compression ratio.
notes: Simulation. Multi-channel encoders only degrade more slowly under measurement noise. Negative for generic EO compression: daylight EO is usually high-SNR, where plain binning is as good or better.

claim: Hybrid optical-electronic CNN with an optimized diffractive phase mask (Chang et al., Sci. Rep. 8, 12324 (2018)): prototype accuracy, grayscale CIFAR-10
quote: we achieve a 46.9% accuracy on the validation set and a 44.4% accuracy on the test set.
notes: Simulated optical conv reached 51.0%. Tier next.

claim: Same hybrid CNN: electronic FLOPs left after moving the conv layer into optics
quote: only 180,234 FLOPs are required in the electronic portion of this model, approximately 12% of the 1,490,954 FLOPs required by the fully digital implementation.
notes: Operation count from the simulated model; no energy measured. The camera still digitises the full intermediate image (no conversion removed).

claim: Same prototype's input light: a laser made spatially incoherent with rotating diffusers (emulating natural light)
quote: illuminated by 532 nm laser light (Coherent Inc.) made spatially incoherent by scrambling through two rotating diffusers
notes: Models assumed monochromatic (temporally coherent) but spatially incoherent light; broadband scene light was not tested.

claim: Spatially incoherent diffractive processors can in principle realise any linear intensity transformation, given enough diffractive features (numerical)
unit: diffractive features (Ni, No = input, output pixels)
locator: arXiv abstract (Rahman et al., Light Sci. Appl. 2023)
quote: we numerically demonstrate that a spatially-incoherent diffractive network can be trained to all-optically perform any arbitrary linear intensity transformation between its input and output
notes: Condition 'if N >= ~2 Ni No' follows in the same sentence (math glyphs omitted from the quote). Simulation only. For an EO tile of 110,592 inputs and 564 outputs this is ~1.2e8 features (DERIVED: 2 x 110,592 x 564).

claim: Photon-aware neuromorphic sensing (PANS, Cornell 2026): classification with a handful of detected photons per inference
unit: percent accuracy / detected photons per inference
quote: 86% (97%) on MNIST with 8.6 (29) detected photons
notes: Active structured illumination from a smartphone OLED array (incoherent) and single-photon detection. Shows the information floor is far below camera photon counts, but it is a lab few-photon regime, not bright EO imagery.

claim: 2D-material (WSe2) photodiode array that is itself a neural network (Mennel et al., Nature 579, 62 (2020)): throughput
quote: successfully train the sensor to classify and encode images, that are optically projected onto the chip, with a throughput of 20 million bins per second.
notes: Input images were laser light shaped by an SLM ('Laser light is linearly polarized by a wire-grid polarizer and reflected by a spatial light modulator'), not incoherent scene light. 9 pixels. Tier speculative for EO.

claim: Analog focal-plane sensor-processor (SCAMP-5) running a CNN in the pixel array (AnalogNet)
value: 96.9% MNIST at 2260 FPS, 0.7 mJ per frame
quote: AnalogNet, reaches a testing accuracy of 96.9% on the MNIST handwritten digits recognition task, at a speed of 2260 FPS, for a cost of 0.7 mJ per frame.
notes: Electronic in-pixel analog compute on incoherent scene light (camera): removes the per-pixel ADC and off-chip transfer, but the photodiode conversion remains. 256x256 pixel-processor array.

claim: Compressive CMOS image sensor that compresses 4x in the analog domain before the ADC (Park et al., IEEE JSSC 56, 2503 (2021)): energy per pixel
quote: The corresponding energy per pixel (51 pJ/pixel) amounts to more than 5x improvement over the previous low-energy benchmark for CS image sensors.
notes: Abstract read via WebFetch (text saved in evidence/sources/R10/webfetch-yonsei-park2021-abstract.txt); full paper paywalled. DERIVED check: 0.7 mW / (640 x 480 x 45 /s) = 50.6 pJ/pixel. Used as the low end of detection+readout energy in the worked example.

claim: Same sensor: compression before digitisation cuts ADC power, data size and I/O power; VGA prototype power
quote: data compression is achieved prior to the pixel digitization, thereby greatly reducing ADC power, data size, and I/O power. ... A prototype VGA image sensor implemented in a 110-nm CMOS process consumes only 0.7 mW at 45 frames/s.
notes: Electronic analog-domain analogue of H2: conversion count reduced 4x before the ADC. Image quality PSNR > 33.7 dB.

claim: Energy to move one byte inside vs out of a CMOS image sensor (CamJ, ISCA 2023)
value: ~1 pJ/B (uTSV, in-stack) vs ~100 pJ/B (MIPI CSI-2 off-chip)
quote: data communication inside a CIS using a uTSV consumes about 1 pJ/B, whereas the energy cost of transmitting one Byte out of the CIS through the MIPI CSI-2 interface consumes about 100 pJ of energy
notes: Literature values cited by CamJ (ref. [49]). Off-sensor transport is ~100x in-sensor; a front end that shrinks the output removes this term.

claim: CamJ (silicon-validated energy model): moving the first image-processing stages from digital to analog in-sensor compute
quote: Moving the first stages of the Ed-Gaze algorithm to the analog domain reduces the energy by 38.8% and 77.1%.
notes: Model validated against 9 measured CIS chips (MAPE 7.5%), but this result is a modelled design point. Savings come from removing ADCs and SRAM.

claim: LightOn Appliance OPU (optical random projection by multiple scattering): vendor throughput and power
value: 1500 TeraOPS at 30 W (50 TeraOPS/W); 1e6 binary in, 2e6 8-bit out, 1.9 kHz
quote: independent computations can be made at 1.9 kHz, for a power consumption of 30 W. It thus reaches 1500 TeraOPS, or 50 TeraOPS / W.
notes: Whole 2U appliance power incl. laser, FPGA I/O, camera. Input is binary (DMD), output 8-bit, fixed random matrix: not a programmable MVM.

claim: DERIVED consistency check of the OPU 1500 TeraOPS figure
value: 3.8e15 MAC/s implied by the stated dimensions vs 1.5e15 OPS stated
quote: In the LightOn Appliance OPU, x (binary) and y (8-bit) scale up to dimension 1 million and 2 million, respectively
notes: DERIVED: 1e6 x 2e6 x 1.9e3 /s = 3.8e15 multiply-adds/s, 2.5x the stated 1.5e15 'OPS'. The paper does not state its op-counting convention, so the vendor figure cannot be reproduced; per-op comparisons with matmul hardware are unreliable.

claim: LightOn OPU vs NVIDIA P100 GPU, random features of dimension D (measured energy)
value: OPU 45 J constant (30 W x 1.5 s); GPU higher from D = 18,000; >10x at D = 58,000
quote: The GPU consumes more than 10 times as much energy as the OPU for D = 58 000 (GPU memory limit). The GPU starts to use more energy than the OPU from D = 18 000.
notes: GPU energy from nvidia-smi; matrix build/load excluded for both. Advantage only at very large projection size.

claim: OPU light path: data are re-encoded onto a coherent laser by a DMD and read by a camera (not light-native input)
quote: The data vector is encoded in the coherent light from a laser using a DMD. Light then goes through a scattering medium and a speckle pattern is measured by a camera.
notes: Conversions: electronic -> DMD -> light -> camera ADC; it adds a DAC/ADC pair rather than removing one. With incoherent scene light a scattering medium gives a non-negative intensity transmission matrix instead of a complex Gaussian one (inferred from R10-021's H = |h|^2; not demonstrated for the OPU).

claim: LightOn transfer-learning example: OPU as a dense layer vs CPU/GPU only
quote: leads to x8 speedups and x11 energy savings compared to the same code on CPU/GPU only, with the same final accuracy.
notes: Vendor example; baseline hardware and energy method not specified.

claim: Amplitude-only Fourier-optics (4f) CNN with DMDs (Miscuglio et al., Optica 7, 1812 (2020)): throughput and accuracy
quote: performing classification tasks on 2-Megapixel large matrices at 10 kHz rates
notes: Coherent HeNe 633 nm laser; lenses do the Fourier transforms passively; camera at 1 kHz limits practice. No energy per operation reported (negative finding). Authors note use when 'the input images are already encoded in a coherent radiation'.

claim: Optalysys (formerly free-space Fourier optics) now markets silicon-photonic compute inside optical data links
value: 384 GOPS per wavelength at 32 GSps; 2.76 pJ/bit link energy excl. laser (estimated)
quote: Native 384 GOPS / lambda @ 32GSps (GF45nm) ... Estimated 2.76 pJ/bit link energy on 45nm silicon photonics, excluding laser.
notes: Data already in light, but in fibre (comms), not scene light. That the company no longer sells free-space Fourier processors is inferred from this page only. Out of R10 scope beyond this pointer (R9).

claim: Sentinel-2 MSI raw source data rate and on-board compressed rate
quote: The PLDHS (Payload Data Handling System) provides source data compression from 1.3 Gbit/s to 450 Mbit/s
notes: Agency/prime design value. Lossy wavelet compression (~2.9x).

claim: Sentinel-2 X-band payload downlink rate
locator: eoPortal Sentinel-2, overview and RF communications table
quote: The platform provides X-band MSI data downlink at 560 Mbit/s
notes: Raw MSI rate (1.3 Gbit/s) is 2.3x the downlink rate; compression is mandatory. Plus EDRS optical relay (R10-041).

claim: Sentinel-2 daily data volume per satellite after on-board compression
quote: Each Sentinel-2 satellite collects 1.5 TB/day, after onboard compression.
notes: Contradiction: the same page says '1.6 TB of data per orbit' (R10-039); at ~14 orbits/day those cannot both be bytes. Unit ambiguity (TB vs Tbit) unresolved.

claim: Sentinel-2 carpet-mapping data volume per orbit
quote: The 'carpet mapping' imaging plan requires the acquisition, storage and transmission of 1.6 TB of data per orbit.
notes: Inconsistent with R10-038 and with the 2.4 Tbit mass memory; treat as an order-of-magnitude statement.

claim: Sentinel-2 MSI instrument power and data quantisation
locator: eoPortal Sentinel-2, spacecraft section and Table 5 (MSI instrument parameters)
quote: The S/C power is 1700 W max, including approximately 170 W for the MSI ... Data quantization 12 bit Instrument mass, power ~290 kg, < 266 W
notes: Two different MSI power figures on the same page; the range 170-266 W is carried.

claim: Sentinel-2 alternative downlink via the EDRS optical/Ka relay
quote: EDRS operates at bit rates of 600 Mbit/s and higher.
notes: Laser LEO-GEO link; relay capacity is shared with Sentinel-1.

claim: DERIVED: Sentinel-2 MSI whole-instrument energy per raw bit and per 12-bit sample
quote: The PLDHS (Payload Data Handling System) provides source data compression from 1.3 Gbit/s to 450 Mbit/s
notes: DERIVED: (170 to 266 W) / 1.3e9 bit/s = 131-205 nJ/bit; x 12 bit = 1.57-2.46 uJ per sample. Whole-instrument average (optics thermal control, SWIR cooler, front-end electronics, digitisation, compression), assuming continuous imaging at the raw rate; it is an upper bound on per-sample detection cost, not an ADC energy.

claim: Planet Dove high-speed downlink (HSD) operational pass performance
value: 160 Mbit/s average, 220 peak; 12-15 GB per 7-10 min pass
locator: eoPortal Planet, HSD ground segment section
quote: Typical ground stations passes average at 160 Mbit/s and peak at 220 Mbit/s data rates with data volumes of 12-15 GB downloaded per 7-10 minute ground station pass.
notes: Operational fleet statistics from Planet's SmallSat 2017 paper as reproduced by eoPortal (primary PDF blocked by Cloudflare).

claim: Planet HSD2 X-band transmitter (3U CubeSat): DC power and maximum on-orbit rate
value: 50 W DC; 1674 Mbit/s max on orbit; 6 channels of 37-336 Mbit/s; RF 1 W per polarisation
quote: DC power consumption 50 W ... Maximum data rate achieved on orbit 1674 Mbit/s (at the time of publication)
notes: Table values; the 1674 Mbit/s is an on-orbit achievement, the 50 W is a specification.

claim: DERIVED: radio energy per downlinked bit, Planet HSD2 at maximum rate
quote: DC power consumption 50 W ... Maximum data rate achieved on orbit 1674 Mbit/s
notes: DERIVED: 50 W / 1.674e9 bit/s = 29.9 nJ/bit. Lower bound for this radio (at lower rates the energy per bit rises). Transmitter only; ground segment excluded.

claim: Planet constellation daily downlink volume
quote: achieve record downlink speeds of 220 Mbit/s and data volumes of over 4 TB/day.
notes: Constellation-wide, ~2017-era HSD1 fleet.

claim: IQ spacecom XLink-X CubeSat X-band transceiver: rate and power
value: up to 200 Mbps; max 16 W (Tx + Rx)
quote: 2 kbps... 200 Mbps ... max 16 W (Tx + Rx)
notes: Buyable CubeSat radio (tier current).

claim: DERIVED: radio energy per downlinked bit, XLink-X at maximum rate and maximum power
quote: max 16 W (Tx + Rx)
notes: DERIVED: 16 W / 200e6 bit/s = 80 nJ/bit (upper-bound power at top rate).

claim: AWS Ground Station antenna-time pricing (Feb 2020 briefing to NASA ESTO)
quote: Pricing based on time of connectivity, not amount of data received ... $10/min $22/min ... $3/min $10/min
notes: Dated price list; charged per minute, not per bit. Narrowband <=54 MHz / wideband >54 MHz in this deck (current page uses 40 MHz).

claim: Current AWS Ground Station pricing page lists no per-minute prices (quote-based)
locator: Pricing page rendered in a browser 2026-09-27
quote: Request a pricing quote
notes: Page rendered with JavaScript: only a glossary (narrowband < 40 MHz, wideband >= 40 MHz) and 'Contact us'. The $/min figures in R10-049 are from 2020 and may be stale.

claim: DERIVED: ground-station cost per GB at Planet-like pass volumes and 2020 AWS prices
quote: Pricing based on time of connectivity, not amount of data received
notes: DERIVED: wideband $/min x pass minutes / GB per pass: on-demand 22 x 7 / 15 = 10.3 to 22 x 10 / 12 = 18.3; reserved 10 x 7 / 15 = 4.7 to 10 x 10 / 12 = 8.3 $/GB. Mixes Planet's own-network pass statistics with AWS prices: illustrative only.

claim: Global cloud fraction from the MODIS cloud mask (King et al., IEEE TGRS 51, 3826 (2013))
quote: Globally, the cloud fraction derived by the MODIS cloud mask is ~67%
notes: Sets the fraction of optical EO scenes a cloud screen can discard (0.67 used in the worked example).

claim: Kodan (ASPLOS 2023) simulation of Landsat 8: share of observable high-value (cloud-free) data a bent pipe can downlink
quote: Accounting for the downlink bottleneck (middle), less than 21% of observable high-value data is downlinked with a bent-pipe.
notes: cote simulator with the real Landsat 8 orbit, WRS frames and ground segment; ~3600 observable frames/day, 1/3 cloud-free. Downlink capacity, not energy, is the first bottleneck.

claim: Kodan: directly deploying a cloud filter on the satellite recovers only a small part of the potential gain because of compute time
value: +9% vs potential 3x; 98 s processing vs 22 s frame deadline
quote: Direct-deployment of cloud filtering improves high-value data downlinked by just 9%, far short of the potential 3x. The shortfall stems from the 98 s frame processing time, which exceeds the 22 s frame deadline
notes: Measured application runtime inside a simulated orbit; hardware for the 98 s figure not restated in that paragraph (evaluation uses Jetson AGX Orin 15 W, R10-055). Once triage is attempted, on-board compute becomes the binding constraint.

claim: Kodan: Jetson AGX Orin 15 W mode taken as the practical ceiling for a 3U CubeSat compute subsystem
quote: in its 15 W power mode - near the maximum reasonable power draw for a 3U cubesat subsystem.
notes: Authors' judgement, not a measured satellite budget.

claim: NASA GSFC: downlink saturation example (MMS science mission)
quote: generates approximately 100 GB/day of science data in its high data rate mode, but only 4% of this data can be transmitted to the ground on average
notes: Not an Earth-observation mission; shows how far generation can exceed downlink.

claim: NASA GSFC: vendor efficiency of COTS edge AI chips flown or tested for space
quote: the Google Coral Edge TPU advertises a performance of 4 trillions of 8-bit integer operations per second at only 2 W
notes: 0.5 pJ/op (DERIVED: 2 W / 4e12). Myriad 2 and Myriad X said to be similar per watt; rad-hard CPUs are about two orders of magnitude worse per watt (same source, Fig. 2).

claim: Phi-Sat-1 (launched 2020): the first on-board CNN inference on a dedicated chip for EO; accelerator power
value: ~1 W nominal at 600 MHz (Myriad 2); EoT board 'well below 2 W'
locator: Giuffrida et al., IEEE TGRS 60, 5517414 (2022), Sec. III-B
quote: it can operate at 600 MHz nominally consuming only 1 W.
notes: Component nominal, not a flight power measurement. Same paper: EoT board 'maintaining the power consumption well below 2 W'. Tier current (flown).

claim: Phi-Sat-1 CloudScout segmentation CNN: inference time per 192x192x3 tile
quote: The inference time is approximately 102 ms exploiting 8 of the 12 available SHAVE vector processors of the Myriad 2, and consuming only 62.9 KB of memory footprint.
notes: Input tensor 192 x 192 x 3 (same section). Where timed (ground bench vs orbit) not stated.

claim: Phi-Sat-1 CloudScout accuracy: pixel-wise and tile-level, false positives (synthetic test set)
quote: the 88.4% of accuracy of the segmentation algorithm corresponds to 95.1% of tiles accuracy with only 0.8% of the images were classified as False Positive
notes: Cloudy tile = >70% cloudy pixels. Test data synthesised from Sentinel-2.

claim: Phi-Sat-1: on-board AI limited to 3 of 10 spectral bands by accelerator memory and the satellite power budget
quote: The CloudScout NN exploits only three of the ten bands available from the HyperScout 2 for two main reasons: memory constraints on the Myriad 2, and power limits derived from the satellite power budget.
notes: Direct evidence that on-board energy, not only downlink, constrains EO triage on small satellites. Also Sec. III: in-flight band reduction 'was deemed prohibitive due to the necessary power required'.

claim: HyperScout-2 (Phi-Sat-1/-2 imager) peak and processing power
quote: Peak power: 12 W Processing power consumption: 6 W
notes: Instrument 1.7 kg, 19 x 13 x 12 cm.

claim: Phi-Sat-1 6U platform battery storage
quote: nominal energy storage of ~46 Wh
notes: At 6 W processing (R10-062) a full battery covers ~7.7 h of processing (DERIVED: 46 / 6), before bus loads.

claim: In-orbit measurement (BUPT-1, 12U, MobiCom 2024): share of satellite energy consumed by COTS computing tasks
quote: there is a 30% to 40% energy consumption occupied by the computing tasks while the communication power consumption and others power consumption remain stable.
notes: Raspberry Pi 4B and Huawei Atlas 200 DK payloads; 6 months of telemetry. Battery 2 x 115 Wh; data downlink 100 Mbps (Table 1).

claim: BUPT-1: sustained compute overheats the payload
value: ~9 W for 10 h exceeds the 30 C operating limit
quote: A computation task lasting 10 hours, operating at approximately 9 Watts, causes the surface temperature to rise beyond the operational limit
notes: Passive heat rejection only; thermal, not just energy, caps on-board compute.

claim: BUPT-1: computing drives battery depth of discharge beyond safe margins
quote: the power consumption of COTS computing devices can have a significant impact on the battery's Depth of Discharge (DoD), potentially causing it to exceed 30%, even 50%.
notes: Paper: raising average DoD from 25% to 30% can cut battery life ~25%.

claim: FOOL (2025): a Sentinel-2-like CubeSat sensor would need its data cut 4.5x to fit a WorldView-3-class link per pass
value: 410 GB per pass vs 90 GB link per pass (4.5x)
quote: using a higher-end link, such as WorldView-3 [29] where Vlink = 90 GB per pass, the enc needs to decrease the data volume by a factor of 4.5.
notes: Hypothetical sensor configuration; illustrates the downlink gap. Same paper cites the Dove HSD 'segments with volumes as low as 12 GB during a single ground station pass'.

claim: BUPT-spectra01 (launched 2024-11-11): snapshot compressive hyperspectral payload - optical coding compresses 47 bands onto one detector frame before readout
value: 47x data compression; 47 bands, 400-700 nm, 6.5 nm; 1 ms exposure; 30 fps
quote: Through a single exposure (1 ms), the payload enables 47-band hyperspectral imaging with a spectral resolution of 6.5 nm, achieving 47-times data compression simultaneously.
notes: The only flown optical preprocessing-before-detection for EO found. Incoherent sunlight; coding by a reflective mask + prism (intensity-domain, non-negative). Conversions removed: 46 of 47 readouts vs a full-cube capture at the same spatial sampling. Reconstruction by a neural network (SSI-Net); where it runs is not stated in the text read (likely ground - inferred). Tier current (flown).

claim: BUPT-spectra01 payload size and mass
value: 182 x 214 x 94 mm; 1.535 kg; 50 m GSD; 51 x 64 km swath
quote: achieve high compactness (182 mm x 214 mm x 94 mm, 1.535 kg) and low cost
notes: No payload power figure found in the main text (negative finding).

claim: BUPT-spectra01 in-orbit ground-cover classification accuracy (K-means on reconstructed cube vs manually annotated map, Abu Dhabi)
quote: accuracy of 80.493%. According to the classification results, we plot the reconstructed spectra of five types of ground cover.
notes: Unsupervised K-means, 5 classes; no all-electronic (full-cube) baseline on the same scene.

claim: TU Berlin in-orbit optical AI payload concept (CEAS Space J. 2025): purpose is cloud filtering before downlink
quote: Images containing clouds will be filtered before the downlink, leaving only unobstructed views of the Earth.
notes: Laser + SLM free-space vector-matrix multiplier -> camera; later MZI network. The image is digitised first and re-encoded on a laser: no photon->electron conversion is removed. Tier speculative.

claim: Same concept: preliminary 4x4 optical vector-matrix multiply accuracy; energy not considered
quote: In our current free-space setup, energy consumption is neglected for the time being.
notes: Accuracy quote: 'The first results show an accuracy of 84.5 %'. No energy data (negative finding).

claim: Follow-on proof of concept (CEAS Space J., 9 Mar 2026): MZI-network optical convolution, MNIST subset
quote: Experiments on a limited subset of MNIST achieved a classification accuracy of 93.3% using the optical system, compared to 96.6% on conventional hardware.

claim: DERIVED: radiance of a sunlit perfectly white Lambertian scene relative to the solar disc
quote: defined the astronomical unit to be a conventional unit of length equal to 149 597 870 700 m exactly.
notes: DERIVED: theta = R/au = 6.957e8 / 1.49598e11 = 4.650e-3 rad; Omega = pi theta^2 = 6.794e-5 sr. Scene spectral radiance L = rho E / pi with E = L_sun Omega (normal incidence), so L/L_sun = rho Omega/pi <= 2.163e-5 for rho <= 1. Atmosphere and oblique sun only lower it.

claim: DERIVED (via D18): optical power per spatial mode collectable from a sunlit white scene
value: <= 1.39 pW per THz at 1,550 nm; <= 0.170 pW per THz (4.7e5 photons/s) at 550 nm
unit: W per mode per THz (both polarisations)
quote: defined the astronomical unit to be a conventional unit of length equal to 149 597 870 700 m exactly.
notes: DERIVED: P_mode = 2 n hv dnu, n = 1/(exp(hv/kT)-1), T = 5772 K. 1,550 nm: n = 0.2504, P_sun = 64.2 nW/THz (= D18) x 2.163e-5 = 1.39 pW/THz. 550 nm: hv = 2.254 eV, n = 0.01087, P_sun = 7.86 nW/THz x 2.163e-5 = 0.170 pW/THz = 4.70e5 photons/s per THz. Upper bound (rho = 1, no atmosphere).

claim: DERIVED: rate at which one single-mode input (waveguide) can deliver 8-bit shot-noise-limited reads of a sunlit scene
value: <= ~72 reads/s per mode per 10 THz of optical bandwidth (550 nm)
quote: defined the astronomical unit to be a conventional unit of length equal to 149 597 870 700 m exactly.
notes: DERIVED: 8-bit needs 4^8 = 65,536 photons (D11, QE = 1). 4.70e5 photons/s/THz x 10 THz = 4.70e6 /s -> 13.9 ms per read (~72 reads/s); 100 THz -> 1.4 ms. So GHz-clocked single-mode photonic meshes cannot run on scene light; only massively multimode free-space optics with large-etendue detectors can. Consistent with D18/E018 for sunlight.

claim: DERIVED: incoherent fan-in into one single-mode output is lossy; intensity-domain weights are non-negative
value: output = sum_i |U_ji|^2 I_i with sum_i |U_ji|^2 = 1 -> uniform N-way combining keeps 1/N
locator: Supplementary Note 2 (non-negativity); unitarity argument in notes
quote: the modulation of the intensity of a spatial mode by an LCD pixel corresponds to product between two non-negative numbers
notes: DERIVED: a passive lossless N x N network is unitary U; for mutually incoherent inputs the cross terms average to zero, so output port j receives sum_i |U_ji|^2 I_i with row sum 1 -> equal weights keep 1/N of the total. Lossless summation of N incoherent pixels therefore needs a detector with >= N modes of etendue (free-space, large-area detector), not a single-mode waveguide. Negative weights need differential detection (two outputs).

claim: DERIVED worked example (100 tiles, 67% cloudy): on-board energy, electronic triage (B) vs optical triage before detection (C)
quote: The inference time is approximately 102 ms exploiting 8 of the 12 available SHAVE vector processors of the Myriad 2
notes: DERIVED per 100 tiles, N = 110,592 samples/tile. Readout E_r = 51 pJ (R10-025) to 1.57-2.46 uJ (R10-042). B = 100 N E_r + CNN (10.2-20.4 J) + downlink 33 tiles (1.31 J HSD2 / 3.50 J XLink-X): low end 0.56 mJ + 10.2 + 1.31 = 11.5 J; high end 27.2 + 20.4 + 3.5 = 51.1 J. C = encoder reads 100 x 564 x E_r (2.9 uJ-0.14 J) + gated readout of 33 clear tiles (0.19 mJ-9.0 J) + same downlink: 1.3 J to 12.6 J. ASSUMPTIONS: passive optical encoder at 196:1 (R10-002) reaching CloudScout-grade decisions (unproven), region-gated readout of the imaging sensor, negligible digital back end, light split between branches ignored. Saving is dominated by removing the CNN (and, for flight instruments, skipping cloudy readouts).
